players.note: DeVonta Smith didn't have a massive Week 1 as the WR45 in weekly scoring. Hurts only threw the ball 25 times against the Commanders, so Smith's 20% target share (tied for the team lead) with a 23.5% first-read share didn't seem great. Smith finished with only three receptions and 53 receiving yards (1.83 YPRR, third on the team). Smith did see a deep target, but he didn't garner any red zone or end zone targets. Smith might not see a huge influx of volume in Week 2, but against the Titans he could easily be a WR2. In Week 1, Tennessee allowed the eighth-most fantasy points per target and the second-most yards per target to perimeter wide receivers. Cordale Flott and Alontae Taylor weren't a formidable outside duo for Tennessee in Week 1, allowing a 118.8 passer rating and a 75% catch rate combined.

DJ Moore crushed all expectations in Week 1 as the Bills' new alpha wide receiver. He was the WR9 in weekly scoring, leading the team with a 24.1% target share and 33.3% first-read share while posting 100 receiving yards and three deep targets (zero red zone/end zone targets). I expect Moore to eat again in Week 2 against a Detroit secondary that allowed the 11th-most fantasy points per target and the seventh-most yards per target to perimeter wide receivers in Week 1.

In Week 1, after much speculation, Malik Nabers played and played well. He had only a 69.7% route share and 54.4% snap rate, but he turned that into a 31% target share and 36.4% first-read share. Nabers churned out 69 receiving yards and 3.0 yards per route run while drawing a red zone target. Nabers should see his playing time increase slightly in Week 2. With that bump in routes and his strong per-route efficiency, I wouldn't be shocked to see him produce as a WR2 this week. Last week, the Rams allowed the 12th-most yards per target and the fourth-most fantasy points per target to perimeter wide receivers.

Rashee Rice had a touchdown in Week 1 to save his disappointing fantasy day as the WR36 for the week. Rice was almost a forgotten piece of the passing attack with a 7.4% target share (3.5 aDOT), 19 receiving yards (0.70 YPRR), one red zone target, and a 10% first-read share. His first-read share was third on the team behind Xavier Worthy and Travis Kelce. We'll see if Rice can bounce back this week against an Indy secondary that allowed the most yards per target and the second-most fantasy points per opportunity to receivers in Week 1, but I'm not hopeful. Rice is a low aDOT drag route artist in what looks like a low or middling passing volume offense. This could be a high-volume passing offense again as Patrick Mahomes gets healthier and so does his offensive line as we move through the season, but I don't think we see that change in Week 1.

The 49ers' usage of their players was weird in some aspects in Week 1 because of the one-sided nature of the game, as they crushed the Rams. Mike Evans finished as the WR14 in weekly scoring, but he had only a 63.9% route share. This could also be related to the fact that Evans dealt with some nagging soft tissue stuff during camp, and San Francisco didn't want to run him out there for a 90% route share in Week 1. Evans still tied for the team lead with a 20.6% target share while producing 49 receiving yards (2.16 YPRR) and seeing a team-leading 24% first-read share. Evans was second on the team with two red zone targets. I don't expect the Miami Dolphins' youthful secondary to be able to contain Evans in Week 2. The Raiders didn't have to test them much in Week 1 and don't have the players to do so even if they wanted to. If Evans had his way with the Rams, I don't expect the Dolphins to be much of a problem.

In Week 1, Parker Washington operated as Jacksonville's WR1, finishing as the WR11 for the week. Washington had a 26.1% target share, 83 receiving yards (5.53 YPRR), zero red zone targets, two deep targets, and a 27.8% first-read share. The target share and first-read share easily led the team. The last time these two teams met, Washington had a 25% target share, 145 receiving yards, two red zone targets, a 23.8% first-read share, 26.5 PPR points, and a WR3 finish for the week. I expect Trevor Lawrence to lean on Washington again this week in this matchup, with Patrick Surtain likely shadowing Brian Thomas Jr. It won't be an easy matchup, though. Last year, Denver allowed the third-fewest fantasy points per target and the eighth-fewest yards per target to slot receivers.

Drake London will be a tough player to depend upon with Cooper Rush under center. In Week 1, with Cooper Rush operating as Captain Checkdown, London had only a 13.6% target share, 29 receiving yards (1.21 YPRR), zero red zone targets, zero deep targets, and a 21.4% first-read share. There's nothing good to see here. Nothing at all. Rush is a below-league average passer and it showed in Week 1. We'll see if he can bounce back in Week 2 against a Carolina secondary that was leaky in Week 1. Last week, Carolina allowed the sixth-most yards per target to perimeter wide receivers while ranking 15th in passer rating allowed.

Tee Higgins had a quiet week in Week 1 as the WR41 in fantasy. Higgins had a 17.1% target share, 59 receiving yards (1.90 YPRR), zero red zone targets, two deep targets, and an 18.5% first-read share (second on the team). I know Houston allowed the second-most fantasy points per target and the fourth-most yards per target to perimeter wide receivers in Week 1, but I don't expect this to be a wonderful matchup for Higgins in Week 2. Last year, Houston allowed the sixth-fewest yards per target and the seventh-fewest fantasy points per target to perimeter wide receivers. Higgins has the talent and quarterback play to outkick a tough matchup, but don't expect a massive stat line.

Tetairoa McMillanÂ had a solid showing in Week 1 as the WR32 in fantasy. He was second on the team with a 21.1% target share while tying for the team lead in first-read share with 27.3%. McMillan finished with 75 receiving yards (1.92 YPRR), one red zone target, and one deep target. In Week 1, Atlanta had the fourth-highest single-high rate (67.4%). Last year, in Weeks 13-19 against single high, McMillan had a 25% target per route run rate and 2.17 YPRR. In Week 1, against single high, McMillan had only a 13% target-per-route run rate and 0.65 YPRR. I'm not overreacting to his meh usage against this coverage last week. He should see plenty of volume this week to outkick what could be a tougher matchup if Atlanta's secondary can continue what they put on film in Week 1. Last week, Atlanta allowed the fourth-fewest fantasy points per target and the seventh-fewest yards per target to perimeter wide receivers.

Well, it happened in Week 1. DJ Turner shadowed Emeka Egbuka. Turner followed Egbuka on 69% of his routes and limited him to 53 receiving yards in his coverage. Egbuka was the WR29 for the week, seeing a 21.4% target share with 63 receiving yards (2.17 YPRR), one deep target, and a team-leading 25% first-read share. Egbuka could have a wonderful game in Week 2 as the tip of the passing spear for Baker Mayfield, who should be on the warpath against his former team. Last week, the Browns deployed single high at the fifth-highest rate (66.7%). Last week, against single high, Egbuka had a 27% target-per-route run rate and 2.53 yards per route run. In Week 1, the Browns allowed the eighth-most yards per target and the seventh-most fantasy points per target to perimeter wide receivers. Egbuka should feast

Jaylen Waddle had a horrible beginning to his Denver tenure in Week 1. He led the team with a 78.8% route share but saw only a 10.7% target share and 14.3% first-read share as he finished with one reception for two yards. Bo Nix played terribly in Week 1, and Davis Webb stumbled out of the blocks as a playcaller. I'm not laying this pitiful performance at the feet of Waddle. The entire Denver offense was on life support in Week 1. It won't get any easier in Week 2 for them, but I expect (or hope) that they will look at least serviceable this week. In Week 1, Jacksonville utilized two high with 56.7% of their defensive snaps. In 2024-2025, Waddle, against two high, had a 21% target-per-route run rate and 1.87 YPRR. If Nix can get him the ball, Waddle should have a bounce-back week, but I don't expect it to be a massive stat line. Last year, the Jags allowed the third-fewest yards per target and the second-fewest fantasy points per target to slot receivers.

Luther Burden had a quiet week, considering his team put up 59 points in Week 1 as the WR37 in fantasy. Burden had a 17.2% target share, 63 receiving yards (2.42 YPRR), zero red zone targets, zero deep targets, and a 27.8% first-read share (second on the team). Burden ran 53.8% of his routes from the slot. We'll see if his usage increases in Week 2, but the matchup is solid. In Week 1, Brian Flores continued his heavy usage of two-high coverage, deploying it on 67.4% of their defensive snaps (fifth-highest rate). Last year, against two-high, Burden led the team with a 25% target-per-route run rate while posting 1.88 yards per route run (second-best). Burden could be called upon more this week. Another staple of Flores' defense is the blitz. In Week 1, Flores dialed up blitz at an insane 73.9% clip. Last year, against the blitz, Burden was fourth on the team with a 21% target-per-route run rate, but he was only a part-time player. That could change in 2026. Burden won't have it easy, though. Last year, Minnesota allowed the sixth-fewest fantasy points per target and the seventh-fewest yards per target to opposing slot receivers.

Jameson Williams had a ROUGH Week 1 performance, and that's putting it kindly as the WR44 in fantasy scoring. Williams had a 23.1% target share and a fantastic 36% first-read share, but he had two drops and secured only one of his three contested targets. He also had one red zone target and two deep targets. The big takeaway is that his utilization was WONDERFUL, but Williams produced a wet-fart stat line with 45 scoreless receiving yards because of a bad game. This week he'll face a Bills' secondary that utilized two high at the eighth-highest rate in Week 1 (61.9%). Last year, against two high, Williams saw his TPRR fall from 22% (versus single high) to 16% while his yards per route run remained static against both coverage types at 2.15. The drop in usage in the offense is notable, but his strong efficiency against two-high is a positive indicator. One thing that will also be working against Williams in this matchup is possible shadow coverage from Christian Benford. Benford followed Nico Collins on 93.9% of his routes in Week 1, but he allowed Collins to secure six of his nine targets in his coverage for 66 yards and a score. This doesn't tell the entire story for Benford, though, as he also had a 75% blanketed rate against Collins, which is strong. Last year, Benford followed Ja'Marr Chase, Chris Olave, Tetairoa McMillan, Tyreek Hill, Drake London, D.K. Metcalf, Nico Collins, and AJ Brown on at least 60% of their routes. Only McMillan and London surpassed 60 receiving yards in his coverage, and only Olave and Hill scored touchdowns. I don't expect a massive game from Williams in Week 2.

In Week 1, Adams struggled mightily as a fantasy producer because his quarterback couldn't deliver catchable targets. He had a 66.7% catchable target rate which isn't horrible, but it's definitely not great. Adams had a 21.4% target share and 28.6% first-read share in Week 1, which he turned into three receptions and 26 receiving yards (1.30 YPRR). Adams didn't see a red zone or deep target in Week 1. I'm willing to roll Adams out there again depending upon my options in Week 2. He'll face a Giants' secondary that just held CeeDee Lamb, George Pickens, and company to the tenth-fewest fantasy points per target and the fourth-fewest yards per target on the perimeter.

Terry McLaurin had a horrible Week 1 against a stout Philly secondary. McLaurin finished with only two receptions and 14 receiving yards. He drew an 11.8% target share with 0.40 yards per route run, one red zone target, and a 17.4% first-read share. This is a wonderful bounceback spot for McLaurin in Week 2. Last week, Dallas utilized single high with 54.5% of their defensive snaps. Last year, against single high, McLaurin's target per route run rate rose from 20% (against two high) to 28% as he churned out a stellar 2.49 yards per route run. I'm not scared of this Dallas secondary after they allowed the 13th-most fantasy points per target to perimeter wide receivers in Week 1 and ranked 19th in yards per target against the position.

HELLO HELLO HELLO JALEN COKER! Cokeheads unite! Week 1 was our day. It was wonderful to see Coker balling out as the WR1 overall in fantasy for Week 1. Among all wideouts in Week 1 with at least 20 routes, Coker was tenth in separation score and 15th in route win rate. Coker has the talent to succeed this season. That much is very true. Will he be Carolina's leading receiver all season? Eh, let's pump the brakes on that, but Week 1 was a standout performance. Coker led the team with a 23.7% target share while tying Tetairoa McMillan with a 27.3% first-read share. Coker also had three deep targets and one red zone target, which tied or exceeded McMillan's usage in Week 1. Coker finished with 138 receiving yards (3.94 YPRR) and two scores. In Week 1, Atlanta had the fourth-highest single-high rate (67.4%). Last year, in Weeks 13-19 against single high, Coker had a 21% target-per-route run rate and 2.81 YPRR. In Week 1, against single high, Coker had only a 30% target-per-route run rate and 5.10 YPRR. Those are amazing numbers no matter how you slice it. We'll see if Coker can keep the party bus rolling in Week 2, but Atlanta's secondary could bring him back down to earth some if their Week 1 showing was indicative of how we should view them for the rest of the season. Last week, Atlanta allowed the fourth-fewest fantasy points per target and the seventh-fewest yards per target to perimeter wide receivers. After one week of NFL action. I'm not scared of Atlanta's secondary, though.

Stefon Diggs had a solid start to his Washington career as the WR17 in Week 1. Last week, Diggs had a 26.1% target share, 55 receiving yards (2.20 YPRR), one red zone target, a deep target, and a team-leading 26.1% first-read share. Diggs ran 60% of his routes from the slot. Diggs could follow up his productive Week 1 with another solid showing in Week 2 against a Dallas secondary that allowed the seventh-most fantasy points per target and the ninth-most yards per target to slot receivers in Week 1.

Well, the process was right with D.K. Metcalf for Week 1, but it didn't work out. Atlanta heavily utilized single high just like I knew they would (67.4%), and Metcalf saw a 24.4% target share and 39.1% first-read share, but he fell flat with only four receptions and 40 receiving yards (0.98 YPRR). We're going back to the well this week with Metcalf against a Pats defense that utilized single high with 55.6% of their defensive snaps in Week 1. Metcalf could see shadow coverage from Christian Gonzalez in Week 2. Gonzalez followed Jaxon Smith-Njigba on 65.4% of his routes in Week 1, but Smith-Njigba roasted him, securing six of his nine targets with 103 receiving yards and a score. Metcalf isn't the same tier of receiver as Smith-Njigba, so I don't see him having the same success in Week 2. Last year, Gonzalez followed Emeka Egbuka, Jerry Jeudy, Tee Higgins, and Darius Slayton on at least 60% of their routes, and only Egbuka surpassed 30 receiving yards in his coverage (only Slayton had a receiving touchdown). I expect Metcalf to get featured again this week, but I struggle to see him popping off with a massive week.

Chris Godwin disappointed me in Week 1 considering the matchup. Godwin had only a 14.3% target share, 40 receiving yards (1.33 YPRR), zero red zone targets, zero deep targets, and a 20% first-read share. It was only one game, but it's possible Godwin is cooked at this point in his career. In Week 1, among 72 qualifying receivers, he ranked 69th in separation and 52nd in route win rate. That's horrible no matter how you slice it, but it's only one game. We'll see how Godwin does with some more games under his belt. Godwin has another nice matchup in Week 2, as Cleveland allowed the most fantasy points per target and yards per target to slot receivers in Week 1.

Rome Odunze entered last week's game at less than 100% and it showed in his production and playing time. He had a 48.6% snap rate and 55.3% route share. I hope both of those numbers climb this week, but we'll have to monitor his practice reports. Odunze finished with only a 10.3% target share, 52 receiving yards (2.48 YPRR), two deep targets, and a 5.6% first-read share. If Odunze is healthy enough, he could see a substantial workload against Brian Flores' two high coverage and blitz heavy nature. In Week 1, Brian Flores continued his heavy usage of two-high coverage, deploying it on 67.4% of their defensive snaps (fifth-highest rate). Last year, against two high, Odunze was second on the team with a 24% target per route run rate and he led the team with 1.89 yards per route run. In Week 1, Flores dialed up blitz at an insane 73.9% clip. Last season, against the blitz, Odunze led the team with a 27.8% target share, 30% target per route run rate, and a 32.1% first-read share. My fingers are crossed that Odunze has a big game in Week 2. Last year, Minnesota allowed the second-most yards per target and the third-most fantasy points per target to perimeter wide receivers.

We'll see if Ladd McConkey plays this week after sustaining a rib injury in Week 1. McConkey didn't practice on Wednesday or Thursday of this week because of that rib issue, but he managed a limited practice on Friday. McConkey has been listed as questionable this week. Last week, in the first three quarters of the game, McConkey was almost the entire Chargers passing attack. Johnston had only a 13.3% target share, eight receiving yards (0.62 YPRR), zero red zone targets, zero deep targets, and an 8.3% first-read share. The Chargers offense as a whole sucked last week, so I hope that Mike McDaniel and company see that what they were doing in Week 1 wasn't working. We shall see. I never assume any rationality with coaching anymore. If Johnston does get more work this week, with McConkey active or not, he should have success. In Week 1, Las Vegas utilized single high with 62.2% of their defensive snaps. Last year, in the 11 healthy games Johnston played, against single high, he posted a 21% target per route run rate and 2.07 yards per route run. Last week, Las Vegas allowed the tenth-fewest yards per target and the second-fewest fantasy points per target to perimeter wide receivers, but I'm not fearful of this secondary after only one game.

Last week, Matthew Golden came out firing as the WR17 for the Week with a 26.2% target share, 95 receiving yards (2.38 YPRR), three red zone targets, one deep target, and a 30.3% first-read share. This week, he'll face a Jets' pass defense that utilized two high at the tenth-highest rate in Week 1 (59%). Last year, Golden was more utilized against two high, with his target-per-route run rate climbing from 14% (against single high) to 21% and his yards per route run increasing to 1.60 (1.34 vs. single high). He won't have an easy matchup, but it's one that he can possibly overcome. Last year, the Jets allowed the eighth-fewest yards per target to perimeter wide receivers while ranking 16th in fantasy points per target allowed to the position.

Deebo Samuel was also only a part-time player in Week 1. Samuel finished as the WR13 for the week, but he had only a 44.4% route share. He made the most of it with a 20.6% target share (tied for the team lead), 48 receiving yards (3.0 YPRR), and a 20% first-read share (tied for second on the team). Samuel got in the end zone while leading the team with three red zone targets. He also got his customary rushing usage, adding a carry for 12 yards on the ground. I expect Samuel to have another strong game in Week 2 against a hapless Miami defense.

In Week 1, Michael Wilson was third on the team with an 18.9% target share as he finished with 56 receiving yards (1.56 YPRR), zero red zone targets, one deep target, and a 25.9% first-read share (second on the team behind only Trey McBride). I don't want to plug Wilson into a fantasy lineup in Week 2 against this vaunted Seattle pass defense. In Week 1, Seattle allowed the 11th-fewest yards per target and the sixth-fewest fantasy points per target to perimeter wide receivers.

Courtland Sutton also had a quiet Week 1 to begin the season as Denver's offense struggled against the Chiefs. Sutton finished with a 14.3% target share, 11 receiving yards (0.48 YPRR), one red zone target, and a 14.3% first-read share. In Week 1, Jacksonville utilized two-high with 56.7% of their defensive snaps. This coverage type isn't great for Sutton's outlook in Week 2. Last year, against two-high, Sutton's target-per-route run rate dropped from 26% (against single high) to 18%, and his yards per route run dipped from 2.32 (against single high) to 1.41. If you can, sit Sutton this week. Last year, Jacksonville allowed the third-fewest yards per target and the eighth-fewest fantasy points per target to perimeter wide receivers.

Well, it was nice to see that Josh Downs was a full-time player in Week 1 as he had an 88.7% snap rate and 85.3% route share, but the offseason narrative about him playing on the perimeter didn't come to fruition as Downs ran 82.8% of his routes from the slot. Downs finished fourth on the team with a 12.9% target share while ranking third in first-read share with 21.1%. He had one deep target but zero red zone targets as he finished with 37 receiving yards (1.28 YPRR, 10.2 aDOT). Downs is a low-end flex play with a tough matchup this week. In Week 1, Kansas City allowed the 13th-fewest yards per target and the eighth-fewest fantasy points per target to slot receivers.

Jakobi Meyers had a quiet Week 1 as Jacksonville crushed the Browns. Meyers had only an 8.7% target share, 40 receiving yards (2.50 YPRR), one end zone target (one score), and a 5.6% first-read share. Meyers was the WR28 in fantasy for Week 1. Last year, in this matchup, Meyers had a 19.4% target share, 45 receiving yards (1.15 YPRR), two red zone targets, one deep target, and a 23.8% first-read share. Meyers got more work with Brian Thomas Jr. seeing Patrick Surtain all game. I expect that to be the case again in Week 2. I don't know how successful Meyers will be, though. Last year, Denver allowed the second-fewest yards per target and the fewest fantasy points per target to perimeter wide receivers.

Marvin Harrison Jr. is a sit until further notice. He was the high aDOT cardio king for Arizona. I don't even have words at this point. This is an insane way to utilize his skill set in this offense, and it's not fantasy-friendly at all. Harrison Jr. had only an 8.1% target share (23.0 aDOT) and 7.4% first-read share. He was out-targeted in Week 1 by Trey McBride, Michael Wilson, Kendrick Bourne, and Jeremiyah Love. At this point, Arizona should just trade him.

Khalil Shakir is a deep league flex only for Week 2. He returned to his usual role in Week 1 that we have seen him garner throughout his career, running 57.1% of his routes from the slot. Shakir had a 65.6% route share, a 20.7% target share, 50 receiving yards (2.38 YPRR), and a 20% first-read share (tied for second on the team with Dalton Kincaid). Shakir didn't get a red zone, end zone, or deep target in Week 1, which isn't surprising. He's an empty-calorie PPR flex that you hope falls into the end zone, but in this high-scoring environment, that could happen in Week 2. In Week 1, Detroit allowed the seventh-most yards per target to slot receivers and ranked 15th in fantasy points per target.

Well, Romeo Doubs didn't exactly have the start to his Pats career that he or we fantasy managers wanted. Doubs laid a goose egg in Week 1 as he failed to secure any of his three targets. With AJ Brown on the shelf, the Pats and Drake Maye will have to lean on him more in Week 2. In Week 1, he had a 69% route share, a 9.1% target share, and a 14.8% first-read share. He saw one red zone target and a deep target. In Week 1, Pittsburgh deployed two high with 57.7% of their defensive snaps (12th-highest rate). Last season, with the Packers against two high, Doubs saw his target-per-route run rate climb from 21% (against single high) to 23% and his yards per route run stay stable at 1.86. Doubs could operate as the Pats' clear WR1 in Week 2. After facing Cooper Rush in Week 1, I don't think there's much to take away from the Steelers against perimeter wide receivers, but last season against them the Steelers allowed the 12th-fewest yards per target while ranking 17th in fantasy points per opportunity. Doubs is a volume-based flex play in Week 2.

Last week, Jordan Addison had a quiet game. Addison had only an 8.3% target share, zero receiving yards, one red zone target, and zero first-reads. In Week 1, Chicago utilized single high at the eighth-highest rate (60.5%). Since 2024, against single high, Addison has had an 18% target-per-route run rate and 1.66 yards per route run. Those are passable numbers, but they aren't something to get overly excited about. Against the Chicago secondary, it might not matter in Week 2, though. In Week 1, Chicago allowed the third-most yards per target and the most fantasy points per target to perimeter wide receivers. Addison is a risky but intriguing flex this week.

Last week, Jayden Reed remained a part-time player for the Packers. Reed had a 55.2% snap rate and 63% route share. He had only a 16.7% target share, 20 receiving yards (0.69 YPRR), a 21.2% first-read share, one red zone target, and zero deep targets. With his limited playing time and standing as the fourth option in the passing attack, he'll remain volatile week-to-week for fantasy purposes. This is a decent week to look at him as a flex option, though. Depending on what your options are at the flex. Last year, the Jets allowed the sixth-most yards per target and the 13th-most fantasy points per target to slot receivers.

Unfortunately, with Cam Ward's disastrous Week 1 performance, Carnell Tate's day against the Jets was sunk. Tate led the team with an 18.8% target share and 31.6% first-read share. He was only able to turn that into four receptions and 38 receiving yards (1.15). Even if Tate has a wonderful Week 1, I wouldn't have a ton of interest in playing him against the Eagles this week, but this entire passing attack is tough to invest in until we see signs of life from Cam Ward. Philly was stellar at defending against perimeter wide receivers last year, and they continued that trend in Week 1. Philly allowed the fifth-fewest fantasy points per target and the sixth-fewest yards per target to outside receivers last week.

In Week 1, Devaughn Vele finished as the WR10 in fantasy as Tyler Shough passed early and often, trying to keep up with Detroit. Vele's nine targets look nice on paper until you realize that Shough chucked it 56 times and Vele had a 16.1% target share with 69 receiving yards (1.25 yards per route run). Vele was second on the team with a 22% first-read share with one red zone and one deep target. The inflated passing volume helped puff up Vele's box score, but his per-route numbers were just okay. Vele is a decent flex this week, but the matchup is tougher. In Week 1, Baltimore allowed the 12th-fewest fantasy points per target to slot receivers while ranking 17th in yards per target allowed to the position.

Wan'Dale Robinson also had a sleepy Week 1, with Cam Ward struggling. Robinson tied for the team lead with an 18.8% target share and a 21.1% first-read share (second behind Carnell Tate). He was able to turn that volume into only five receptions and 38 receiving yards (1.15 YPRR). Robinson didn't see a red zone or deep target in Week 1. I don't want to plug Robinson into any lineup in Week 1 despite Cooper DeJean (75% catch rate and 140.6 passer rating allowed) struggling out of the gate last week. I expect Ward to be in a blender this week, and those struggles to continue to tank the receiving options in this passing attack.

In Week 1, KC Concepcion had an 18.2% target share and 28.6% first-read share, which were tied for the team lead with Denzel Boston. Concepcion had a deep target and finished with four receptions and 43 receiving yards (1.95 YPRR). Concepcion was the WR51 for the week. He could have a more productive Week 2, facing a secondary that allowed the 11th-most yards per target and fantasy points from receiving yards per game in Week 1.

In Week 1, Alec Pierce had a 58.5% snap rate and 64.7% route share, which is about where I figured he'd be coming off a lost training camp and preseason as he made his way back from injury and surgery in the offseason. Pierce tied for the team lead with a 19.4% target share (27% TPRR, led the team) and led the team with a 31.6% first-read share. He had a 17.1 aDOT, which I don't think will continue throughout the season if he's going to continue to operate as the team's WR1. Pierce finished with 61 receiving yards (2.77 YPRR), one red zone target, and one deep target as the WR34 for the week. Pierce should see his playing time increase slightly in Week 2 as the team continues to ramp him up. He could be a volume-based flex/WR3 for Week 2 with a tough matchup. In Week 1, Kansas City allowed the 12th-fewest fantasy points per target and the second-fewest yards per target to perimeter wide receivers.

Brian Thomas Jr.Â is dealing with a shoulder injury. He practiced in a limited fashion all week and doesn't carry an injury designation into this game. He opened the week with a limited practice session on Wednesday. Last week, he had only a 50% route share, 13% target share, 40 receiving yards (3.33 YPRR), and a 16.7% first-read share. Even if he was fully healthy, I wouldn't want to play him this week. Last year, when Denver and Jacksonville tangled, Thomas Jr. was shadowed by Patrick Surtain, and I expect that to be the case again this week. Last year, Surtain followed Thomas Jr. on 78.8% of his routes, limiting him to one target, one reception, and nine receiving yards. Sit Thomas Jr. this week. He'll likely get blanketed again by Surtain this week.

Xavier Worthy didn't do much with his opportunities in Week 1, but it's notable that he led the team with a 22.2% target share and 30% first-read share (7.0 aDOT). Worthy was only able to finish with 18 receiving yards (0.67 YPRR), one red zone target, and one deep target. Worthy could be the team's WR1 if this usage holds this season, which would be a passing of the torch from Rashee Rice to him, but it's just a one-game sample, so I'm not getting ahead of myself. Worthy could offer some flex upside this week against a pass defense that was ripped apart in Week 1 by Lamar Jackson. In Week 1, Indy allowed the most yards per target and the second-most fantasy points per opportunity to receivers.

Caleb Douglas had a strong Week 1 as the WR22 in fantasy. He was second on the team with a 22.2% target share, producing 94 receiving yards, a STRONG 3.13 yards per route run, and seeing a team-leading 35.3% first-read share. He didn't have a red zone target, but he did see a deep target. I don't expect Douglas to produce as a WR2 weekly, but his usage could easily make him a WR3/flex moving forward until he has to fight with Chris Bell for the target throne weekly. The 49ers aren't a frightening matchup for perimeter wide receivers, ranking 16th in yards per target and receiving fantasy points per game allowed to the position after Week 1.

Tre Tucker is the only Raiders wide receiver who had more than a 60% route share last week, so he's the only Raiders receiver making the Primer this week. Tucker had a 13.3% target share, 27 receiving yards (1.0 YPRR), one red zone target, and a 16.7% first-read share. I've never been a Tucker believer. He's better off left on your bench this week. Last week, the Bolts allowed the 13th-fewest fantasy points per target to perimeter wide receivers while ranking 15th in yards per target allowed to the position.

Ladd McConkey left Week1 with a rib injury. He didn't practice on Wednesday or Thursday of this week because of that rib issue, but he managed a limited practice on Friday. He has been listed as questionable this week. His status is up in the air. Even if he's active this week, he's a risk to plug into a fantasy lineup, as any big hit to those ribs could knock him out of the game. In Week 1, in the first three quarters of the game, McConkey had an 85% route share, a 46.7% target share, 82 receiving yards (4.82 YPRR), two red zone targets, a 41.7% first-read share, and zero deep targets. If McConkey is a full-time player in Week 2 with a similar usage pattern to Week 1, he should rip the Raiders apart. In Week 1, Las Vegas allowed the third-most yards per target to slot receivers while ranking 16th in fantasy points per target allowed to the position.

Denzel Boston secured a long garbage-time touchdown in Week 1 to finish as the WR23 in fantasy. Boston had an 18.2% target share and 28.6% first-read share. Both of those marks tied for the team lead. Boston finished with 59 receiving yards (2.19 YPRR, 28.7 aDOT), one red zone target, and two deep targets. Boston could have another solid Week 2 facing a secondary that was 18th in yards per target and 19th in fantasy points per target allowed to perimeter wide receivers in Week 1.

Well, Dontayvion Wicks made the most of his opportunities in Week 1 as DeVonta Smith's running mate. He was the WR21 in Week 1 while seeing a 16% target share (third on the team) with 73 receiving yards (2.70 YPRR), an end zone target (one score), and a 23.5% first-read share. Wicks also led the team with two deep targets (21.5 aDOT). If Hurts is looking to go deep again this week, Wicks could have another nice day. Last week, Tennessee allowed both of their deep targets to be secured while giving up 62 deep passing yards (tenth-most). In Week 1, Tennessee allowed the eighth-most fantasy points per target and the second-most yards per target to perimeter wide receivers. Cordale Flott and Alontae Taylor weren't a formidable outside duo for Tennessee in Week 1, allowing a 118.8 passer rating and a 75% catch rate combined.

Malik Washington operated as Miami's WR2 in Week 1. He finished as the WR58 in fantasy, seeing a 29.6% target share and 23.5% first-read share. Washington led the team with three deep targets, but he didn't see a red zone look. Unfortunately, despite the volume, Washington's inefficiencies have followed him into 2026 with only 53 receiving yards and 1.47 yards per route run. Washington is a deep league flex only and more so for PPR formats where his raw volume can play up a tad more. Sit Washington unless you're truly desperate for points. The 49ers allowed the seventh-fewest yards per target and the second-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to receivers in Week 1.

Keenan Allen was a full-time player for the Colts in Week 1 with a 73.5% route share (67.9% snap rate). He was tied for the team lead with a 19.4% target share and was second on the team with a 26.3% first-read share. Allen finished with 32 receiving yards (1.28 YPRR), one red zone target, and zero deep targets as he ran 72% of his routes from the perimeter. Allen is a middling flex play this week with a tough matchup. In Week 1, Kansas City allowed the 12th-fewest fantasy points per target and the second-fewest yards per target to perimeter wide receivers.

Last week, Adonai Mitchel had a 12.5% target share, a 76.9% route share, 60 receiving yards (3.0 YPRR, 19.0 aDOT), one deep target, and a 12.5% first-read share. He faces a Green Bay secondary this week that utilized two high at the highest rate in the NFL in Week 1 (80%). Last year, against two high, Mitchell had a 22% target-per-route run rate, but he had only 1.48 yards per route run. There will be weeks to consider Mitchell as a flex option, but Week 2 isn't one of them.

Last week, Makai Lemon was Philly's starting slot receiver (64.3% slot). While he only played 66% of the snaps, he had an 84.8% route share, so he was on the field when Philly was looking to pass which honestly is good for Lemon, but not great for Philly. If defenses are looking for a tell for when Philly is looking to pass, Lemon could be an easy one to spot with this split if his overall playing time doesn't increase in Week 2. Lemon had only a 16% target share while seeing only manufactured targets around the line of scrimmage. Lemon had a -0.25 aDOT with three receptions, five receiving yards, and 50% of his targets coming on designed looks. In a low passing volume offense, Lemon isn't even flex worthy with this type of usage. I hope his role continues to evolve, but if this is how his usage remains all season he'll be tough to trust even in a flex spot. Sit Lemon in Week 2.

In Week 1, Kayshon Boutte had only a 64.3% route share, a 5.3% target share, and 21 receiving yards (0.78 YPRR) as he was the field stretcher (16.0 aDOT). This isn't the matchup to consider flexing Boutte, hoping that he converts a downfield target to fantasy goodness. Last year, Cincy allowed the fifth-lowest passer rating, the tenth-lowest passing success rate, and the tenth-lowest completion rate to deep passing.

Mack Hollins had his moments in Week 1 with a 70% snap share, 50% route share, a 24% target-per-route run rate, 51 receiving yards, 2.43 yards per route run, and a 19% first-read share. He had one red zone target and one deep target. Hollins could be called upon even more in Week 2. In Week 1, Pittsburgh deployed two high with 57.7% of their defensive snaps (12th-highest rate). Last year, against two high, Hollins saw his target-per-route run rate jump from 18% (against single high) to 22%, and his yards per route run climbed from 1.48 (against single high) to 1.94. Hollins could be the clear number two option in the Pats' passing attack this week. Despite a tough matchup, he has some sneaky flex appeal this week. After facing Cooper Rush in Week 1, I don't think there's much to take away from the Steelers against perimeter wide receivers, but last season against them, the Steelers allowed the 12th-fewest yards per target while ranking 17th in fantasy points per opportunity.

I was shocked in Week 1 to see Kendrick Bourne handing a 21.6% target share (second on the team) and 22.2% first-read share (third on the team). Bourne secured all eight of his targets, churning out 75 receiving yards (2.59 YPRR) while seeing a red zone target. He was the WR17 for the week. If Bourne keeps this type of usage up, he'll have some flex-worthy weeks this season, but I don't think Week 2 will be one of those weeks. Last week, Seattle allowed the third-fewest fantasy points per target and the fourth-fewest yards per target to slot receivers.

Chris Bell isn't startable in fantasy yet. He's only a stash as Miami ramps up his playing time. In Week 1, he had a 51.4% route share, a 7.4% target share, and a 5.9% first-read share. Bell could eventually be the clear number one target for this passing attack as we move through the season, but we're not there yet. Bell is a weekly sit until we see his usage trend up more.

Kalif Raymond popped off with a surprising stat line in Week 1 as the WR15 in fantasy. He had only a 60% snap share and 57.9% route share, but he saw a 31% target share and 33.3% first-read share. Raymond finished with 84 receiving yards, 3.82 YPRR, one red zone target, and one deep target. I don't know if he will or can repeat this type of production, especially with a limited route share, but it's possible that he can. In Week 1, Brian Flores continued his heavy usage of two-high coverage, deploying it on 67.4% of their defensive snaps (fifth-highest rate). Last year, against two-high, Raymond had only a 14% target per route run rate and 1.28 yards per route run, but this was with Detroit. In 2024, with the Lions and Ben Johnson against two-high, Raymond had only a 12% target-per-route-run rate and 0.67 yards per route run. The analytics aren't in Raymond's favor to continue his hot start to the 2026 season. If you're in a deep league or desperate for a flex, I get it, but in most formats and leagues I'm not starting Raymond in Week 2. The matchup could be fruitful if you do decide to turn to Raymond, though. Last year, Minnesota allowed the second-most yards per target and the third-most fantasy points per target to perimeter wide receivers.
